_source: Transcribed from the GWMS Curriculum Guide in Notion. Per-session fields come from that session's Lesson and Intervention Guide (Unit 7). Card, domain and keyCondition come from the GWMS Technical Map. Where the two name the game differently, the Lesson and Intervention Guide wins, because it is the per-session authority.

stage.name: The Initiation
stage.grapplingTlo: By the end of the Initiation, participants will apply chest-pin control and its owned finishes to make contact, hold it under resistance, and reset cleanly after a break, releasing on every tap.
stage.caselTlo: By the end of the Initiation, participants will apply social awareness and relationship skills to make real contact with others, tolerate friction, own their part in a rupture, and attempt repair.
stage.connection: Chest-to-chest contact, friction, break, and reset on the mat is contact, friction, rupture, and repair between people. The Initiation tests the real self against others.

wrongAnswers.text: Holding the finish after your partner taps
wrongAnswers.feedback: Never. Every finish is released instantly on the tap, every time. The tap is law.
You keep the pin by feeling your partner and adjusting, not by clamping and squeezing. Staying calm and adjusting beats forcing harder.

sessions.probingQuestion: What happens in you when someone makes real contact?
sessions.keyCondition: Chest on chest with hips and shoulders covered, three-count.
sessions.gameName: Chest to Chest Under Elbows Maintenance
sessions.gameText: The top player holds chest on chest, under both elbows. Win by keeping that contact for a three-count while the bottom player moves.
sessions.gameNote: This is the most direct contact there is, chest to chest, face to face. Making it and holding it is the mat version of letting someone close.
sessions.gameWin: Keeping chest-on-chest contact under both elbows for a three-count
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will apply chest-to-chest control to make and hold contact with a partner under light resistance.
grapplingElos: Demonstrate a chest-pin control position and hold it for a three-count against light resistance.
Maintain safe, controlled contact with a partner during live rolling without disengaging.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name one thing that happens in them when another person makes real contact, and connect it to how they meet people in real life.
caselElos: Identify one internal reaction, physical or emotional, that comes up during close contact.
Connect that reaction to how they meet people outside the room.
sessions.connection: Holding contact on the mat and noticing what contact does to you are the same skill: staying present when another person is close instead of shoving them away. The pin teaches the body to stay. The reflection teaches the mind to notice why staying is hard.

sessions.probingQuestion: How much of someone else do you actually let in?
sessions.keyCondition: Keep the coverage as the partner moves.
sessions.gameText: The top player keeps the elbows off the body as the partner frames and tries to make space. Win by keeping the elbows controlled continuously.
sessions.gameNote: You keep the pin by feeling your partner and adjusting, not by clamping and squeezing, which is the same as how much you actually let someone in.
sessions.gameWin: Keeping the elbows controlled continuously as the partner frames and moves
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will apply chest-pin control while reading and adjusting to a partner's movement, keeping the pin as the partner works to create space.
grapplingElos: Maintain chest-pin control for a three-count while the partner actively frames and moves.
Adjust pressure and connection in response to the partner rather than forcing a fixed grip.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will identify how much they open up to another person and name one thing that makes letting someone in hard.
caselElos: Notice their own guardedness or openness during close contact.
Name one thing that makes letting another person in difficult.
sessions.connection: Keeping a pin means feeling your partner and adjusting to them, not clamping down and ignoring them. Letting someone in works the same way. You hold the connection by reading the other person, not by walling off and muscling through.

sessions.probingQuestion: Who are you with other people, now that you've met yourself?
sessions.gameText: From the top, stay under both elbows and keep the connection alive as the partner works. It is continuous, no single finish, just holding real contact.
sessions.gameNote: As the real you, not a performance. That is who you are with other people now.
sessions.gameWin: Staying under both elbows and keeping the connection alive continuously
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will establish and keep chest-pin control from a neutral start, rolling as the real self rather than a performance.
grapplingElos: Enter and secure a chest pin from a neutral position.
Keep control without abandoning the position when it gets hard.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will describe who they are with other people now that the Descent named the real self.
caselElos: Name one way the real self shows up differently with others than the old mask did.
Connect that to how they want to be in their relationships.
sessions.connection: The Descent found the real you. Now it goes to the mat with a partner. Rolling as the real self instead of the persona is the same move as showing up honest in a relationship instead of performing one.

sessions.probingQuestion: What do you do when someone pushes back?
sessions.keyCondition: Hold the pin against active resistance, the partner running 4S.
sessions.gameName: Mounted and Side Control Pin Game
sessions.gameText: The top player holds the pin against a partner actively working to escape. Win with hip coverage, under the elbow, and hands connected, all at once, held against real resistance.
sessions.gameNote: Pushback is the trial. Staying calm and adjusting beats forcing harder.
sessions.gameWin: Hip coverage, under the elbow, and hands connected all at once, against real resistance
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will maintain chest-pin control against a partner's active resistance.
grapplingElos: Keep the pin for a three-count while the partner actively resists and works to escape.
Respond to resistance with base and adjustment, not panic or raw force.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what they do when another person pushes back, and judge whether it serves them.
caselElos: Identify their default response to pushback.
Judge whether that response helps or hurts the relationship.
sessions.connection: A partner resisting the pin is pushback made physical. What you do when they fight the pin is usually what you do when people push back in life. Both reward staying calm and adjusting over forcing harder.

sessions.probingQuestion: Can you stay present when it gets uncomfortable?
sessions.keyCondition: Isolate a limb and keep it isolated while the partner works to reconnect it.
sessions.gameText: The top player isolates and pins a wrist while the partner works to free it. Win by keeping the isolation and reaching head-and-arm or chest-to-back contact.
sessions.gameNote: You are staying in an uncomfortable spot and working it instead of bailing out.
sessions.gameWin: Keeping the wrist isolated and reaching head-and-arm or chest-to-back contact
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will stay in a hard chest-pin exchange under discomfort instead of bailing out of the position.
grapplingElos: Remain in a difficult chest-pin position, being framed and bridged, for a set time without disengaging.
Use a regulation tool, breath or base reset, to stay present under pressure.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will practice staying present in discomfort and name what makes them want to bail.
caselElos: Identify the moment they usually want to leave a hard conversation or situation.
Practice one way to stay present instead of leaving.
sessions.connection: Staying in an uncomfortable pin instead of scrambling out is the body's version of staying in a hard conversation. Both are the same skill: tolerating discomfort without fleeing it.
sessions.note: Staying is the skill, but leaving a harmful situation is wisdom, not failure.

sessions.probingQuestion: What does your friction do to the people across from you?
sessions.keyCondition: Firm control that keeps the partner safe, adjust to the tap.
sessions.gameText: The top player breaks the partner down and controls, hips down, shoulder connected, run with an intensity limit. Win by holding control while keeping the partner completely safe.
sessions.gameNote: You can pin hard and still not hurt them. That choice is yours, every round.
sessions.gameWin: Holding control — hips down, shoulder connected — while keeping the partner completely safe
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will apply chest-pin control at an intensity that keeps the partner safe, controlling their own force deliberately.
grapplingElos: Apply the pin firmly while keeping the partner safe.
Adjust intensity based on the partner's signals and taps.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name the effect their conflict style has on other people and one adjustment they can make.
caselElos: Identify how their friction lands on the person across from them.
Name one adjustment that keeps the friction honest but not harmful.
sessions.connection: You can pin someone hard and still keep them safe. That is control of your own force. Your conflict off the mat lands on real people too, and the same control applies: honest friction, not harm.

sessions.probingQuestion: What breaks in you when a connection breaks?
sessions.keyCondition: A frame comes before the bridge, reset cleanly after the break.
sessions.gameText: This one is from the bottom. The pin breaks, you got reversed or stuck underneath. Win by framing first, then standing and turning to face.
sessions.gameNote: Reset clean, no retaliation. That is how you handle a break when a connection goes bad.
sessions.gameWin: Framing first, then standing and turning to face — a clean reset
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will recognize when chest-pin control breaks and reset to a safe position without panic or retaliation.
grapplingElos: Notice the moment control is lost, a reversal or an escape.
Reset to a neutral, safe position instead of forcing or retaliating.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what breaks in them when a connection ruptures.
caselElos: Identify their internal response when a relationship or connection breaks.
Name whether they tend to retaliate, shut down, or withdraw.
sessions.connection: Losing the pin and getting reversed is a small rupture. How you handle that break on the mat, a clean reset or a retaliation, mirrors how you handle broken connections in life.

sessions.probingQuestion: Have you ever broken something with someone and left it broken?
sessions.keyCondition: The choking-side arm is trapped before the frame closes, released on the tap.
sessions.gameName: Mount Head and Arm Trap Game
sessions.gameText: The first owned finish, a strangle. Trap the head and one arm, hands locked. The choking-side arm has to be trapped before the frame closes, and you release the instant your partner taps, every time.
sessions.gameNote: Power you can apply and then let go of. The tap is the invitation to repair, and this week asks whether you take it.
sessions.gameWin: Trapping the head and one arm with hands locked — and releasing the instant your partner taps
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will apply one owned chest-pin finish, a strangle, with full control, releasing the instant the partner taps.
grapplingElos: Secure one owned chest-pin finish under light resistance.
Release instantly and completely on the partner's tap, every time.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name a rupture they left unrepaired, without being required to share it.
caselElos: Acknowledge a broken connection they never repaired.
Notice what leaving it broken has cost them.
sessions.connection: A finish you can apply and release on the tap is power you control. Leaving a break unrepaired is choosing not to release, not to reset. The tap is the invitation to repair. This week asks whether you take it.

sessions.probingQuestion: When something breaks, what part is yours to own?
sessions.keyCondition: Both control points active and the fulcrum set before any extension, released on the tap.
sessions.gameText: The second owned finish, an arm lock. Separate the hands and get two connections to the wrist, both control points set before any extension, released on the tap.
sessions.gameNote: Owning your part when something breaks starts with control, not a yank.
sessions.gameWin: Separating the hands and getting two connections to the wrist, control set before any extension
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will apply a second owned chest-pin finish, an arm lock, with control, and name one thing they did wrong in a round without excuse.
grapplingElos: Secure an owned chest-pin arm lock with control, releasing on the tap.
Name one mistake they made in a round honestly, without blaming the partner.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will identify their own part when something breaks, separate from the other person's.
caselElos: Distinguish their share of a rupture from the other person's.
Name one thing that is theirs to own.
sessions.connection: On the mat you can name your own mistake in a round without blaming your partner. Owning your part of a rupture works the same way. Accountability starts with separating your piece from theirs.

sessions.probingQuestion: What does it take for you to say sorry and mean it?
sessions.keyCondition: Re-engage and re-establish the pin after a scramble.
sessions.gameText: After a scramble, re-establish the pin cleanly. Win by covering the hips, getting under the elbow, and connecting your hands again.
sessions.gameNote: Slap hands and roll clean after a hard round. That reset is repair in the body.
sessions.gameWin: Covering the hips, getting under the elbow, and connecting your hands again after a scramble
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will reset with a partner after a hard exchange and re-establish chest-pin control cleanly.
grapplingElos: Re-engage and re-establish a chest pin after a scramble or reversal.
Roll with a partner right after a heated exchange without carrying it over.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what it takes for them to give a real apology.
caselElos: Identify what a real apology requires of them.
Distinguish a real apology from a dodge.
sessions.connection: Resetting and rolling clean with someone right after a hard round is the body's version of squaring up. A real apology is the same reset: you re-engage instead of carrying the grudge.

sessions.probingQuestion: Can you stay when leaving would be easier?
sessions.keyCondition: Complete a hard round without disengaging, both roles.
sessions.gameName: Guard Recovery with Passing Resistance Game
sessions.gameText: Full live, both roles, against a tough partner. Win, on top, by locking hands and holding the pin against real resistance.
sessions.gameNote: Stay in the hard round and keep working instead of asking to switch. Staying is a choice you make on purpose.
sessions.gameWin: On top, locking hands and holding the pin against real resistance
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will stay with a difficult training partnership and keep working rather than switching out.
grapplingElos: Complete a hard round with a tough partner without disengaging or asking to switch.
Keep control and composure when the partnership is frustrating.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what makes them want to leave a hard relationship and one reason to stay.
caselElos: Identify their exit urge in a hard relationship.
Name one thing worth staying for.
sessions.connection: Staying with a hard partner on the mat instead of switching is commitment made physical. Staying in a hard relationship when leaving is easier is the same choice. Both build the muscle of not bailing on people.
sessions.note: Staying is the skill, but leaving a harmful relationship is not failure. Never taught as an absolute.

sessions.probingQuestion: What does repair cost you, and is it worth paying?
sessions.keyCondition: Flow between control and the owned finishes, tap honored.
sessions.gameName: Hunt for Hips and Shoulders (Perpendicular Start)
sessions.gameText: Open rolling from the chest pin, both sides play. Flow between control and the owned finishes, tap honored, reset and continue.
sessions.gameNote: This is the whole Initiation in one round: contact, friction, a break, and repair.
sessions.gameWin: Flowing between control and the owned finishes with the tap honored, resetting and continuing
sessions.grapplingTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will integrate chest-pin control and finishing in open rolling, using the whole neighborhood in live flow.
grapplingElos: Flow between chest-pin control and owned finishes during live rolling.
Give and honor the tap, resetting and continuing cleanly.
sessions.caselTlo: By the end of this session, the participant will name what repair costs them and weigh whether it is worth paying.
caselElos: Identify the personal cost of repairing a rupture, pride, comfort, or time.
Decide whether repair is worth that cost, and say why.
sessions.connection: Open rolling puts it all together, control, finish, tap, reset, in one flow. Repair is the same integration in relationships: it costs pride and comfort, and you decide it is worth paying. This closes the Initiation and points to the Return.
